n1.point: The investigation covers alleged infringement of U.S. Trademark Registration No. 3,836,415, U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,149,328, and U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,273,875.
n1.quote: infringement of one or more of U.S. Trademark Registration No. 3,836,415 ("the '415 mark"); U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,149,328 ("the '328 mark"); and U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,273,875 ("the '875 mark")

n10.point: The Crocs 3D Marks consist of a three-dimensional shoe design featuring round holes placed across the horizontal portion of the upper and a textured strip along the vertical portion with trapezoidal openings. The '875 Registration also includes a textured strip on the heel and a decorative band along the heel strap.
n10.quote: The Crocs 3D Marks both consist of a three-dimensional configuration of the outside of an upper for a shoe, featuring round holes placed across the horizontal portion of the upper, and a textured strip along the vertical portion of the upper having trapezoidal openings.

n100.point: Walmart argues the Accused Products do not infringe the 3D Marks because: (1) they are not substantially similar; (2) they were designed as generic or basic foam clogs, not to cause confusion or copy the marks; and (3) there is no likelihood of confusion based on multiple factors including dissimilarity, different prices and channels of trade, lack of fame, and multiple coexisting similar uses.
n100.quote: The Accused Products do not infringe the 3D Marks because, among other reasons: (1) the Accused Products are not substantially similar

n101.point: Walmart asserts a Second Defense that the 3D Marks are invalid and unprotectable because they are functional, comprised of non-source-identifying ornamental elements, generic as a shoe style rather than a single source, and lack secondary meaning.
n101.quote: Complainant's 3D Marks are invalid and unprotectable because, among other reasons: (1) the 3D Marks and their use are functional

n102.point: Walmart argues the 3D Marks lack secondary meaning because consumers do not understand the marks as indicating Crocs as the source, and because numerous third parties use substantially similar designs without reference to Crocs as a source.
n102.quote: the 3D Marks lack secondary meaning because consumers do not understand the primary significance of the claimed mark

n103.point: Walmart contends the 3D Marks are comprised of ornamental elements that are not source-identifying and represent a genre or style of shoe rather than a single manufacturer.
n103.quote: the 3D Marks are comprised of various ornamental elements that are not source identifying; (3) the 3D Marks are generic

n104.point: Walmart asserts a Third Defense that the Asserted Trademarks are not famous as defined by federal trademark laws and there is no evidence they are universally recognized by the general consuming public as designating Crocs as the source.
n104.quote: Complainant's Asserted Trademarks are not famous as defined by the federal trademark laws

n105.point: Walmart asserts a Fourth Defense of no dilution, arguing it does not dilute or has not diluted the distinctive quality of any alleged famous trademarks, as the marks lack distinctiveness and are not famous, and the Accused Products are not similar.
n105.quote: Walmart does not dilute and has not diluted the distinctive quality of any alleged famous trademarks of Complainant

n106.point: Walmart asserts a Fifth Defense of failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted.
n106.quote: FIFTH DEFENSE: FAILURE TO STATE A CLAIM Complainant fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted

n107.point: Walmart asserts a Sixth Defense that Crocs has not adequately alleged and cannot establish the existence of a domestic industry for the Asserted Trademarks as required by Section 337(a)(2) and Section 337(a)(3).
n107.quote: Complainant has not adequately alleged and cannot establish the existence of a domestic industry for the Asserted Trademarks

n108.point: Walmart argues Crocs has not satisfied the economic prong of the domestic industry requirement because Crocs failed to establish significant investment in plant and equipment, significant employment of labor or capital, or substantial investment in licensing, research and development, or other qualifying activities relating to the Asserted Trademarks.
n108.quote: Complainant has not and cannot satisfy the economic prong of the domestic industry requirement

n109.point: Walmart asserts that Crocs also has failed to satisfy the technical prong of the domestic industry requirement.
n109.quote: Complainant also has failed to satisfy the technical prong of the domestic industry requirement in this case

n11.point: Complainant asserts U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,149,328 (3D Mark), U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,273,875 (3D Mark with textured heel and decorative band), and U.S. Trademark Registration No. 3,836,415 (CROCS word mark). n148.point: Respondents Walmart Inc., Orly Shoe Corporation, Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., and Quanzhou Zheng De Network Corp. (Amoji) filed a motion on June 10, 2022 seeking an initial determination that Complainant Crocs, Inc.'s asserted trade dress is functional and therefore invalid, and that respondents' accused products cannot infringe the asserted trade dress as a matter of law.
n148.quote: Respondents Walmart Inc., Orly Shoe Corporation, Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., and Quanzhou Zheng De Network Corp., d/b/a Amoji (collectively, "Respondents") filed a motion (Mot. 1 270-054) for summary determination of invalidity due to functionality.

n149.point: Respondents contended that Crocs owns two utility patents showing the claimed shoe design and that the existence of a utility patent is strong and incontrovertible evidence that the claimed trade dress is functional.
n149.quote: Respondents contend that Crocs owns two utility patents showing the claimed shoe design. Mem. at 1. According to Respondents, "[t]he existence of a utility patent is strong and —in this case—incontrovertible evidence that [the] claimed trade dress is functional."

n15.point: Crocs alleges that respondents' accused products infringe the Crocs 3D Marks by copying the design features including the size, positioning, number, and shape of holes on the horizontal portion of the upper, the textured strip along the vertical portion with trapezoidal openings, and the textured strip and decorative band on the heel.
n15.quote: As shown in Figure 3 below, Cape Robbin and Accused Products bear designs that are likely to cause confusion with the Crocs 3D Marks. In particular, the size, positioning, number, and shape of the holes on the horizontal portion of the upper of the Accused Products is confusingly similar to the 3D Marks.

n150.point: The issue is whether Crocs' 3D trade dress marks are functional under the Morton-Norwich test and therefore invalid as a matter of law, such that respondents' accused products cannot infringe.
n150.quote: To assess whether a mark is functional, the Commission applies the Morton-Norwich factors: (1) the existence of a utility patent that discloses th e utilitarian advantages of the design; (2) advertising materials touting the utilitarian advantages of the design; (3) the availability to competitors of functionally equivalent designs; and (4) facts indicating that the design results in a comparatively simple or cheap method of manufacture.

n151.point: The ALJ stated that functionality determinations are based on the whole collection of elements taken together, not individual elements versus overall visual impression.
n151.quote: Functionality determinations are based on "the whole collection of elements taken together." Certain Motorized Vehicles, Comm'n Op. at 16.

n152.point: The ALJ found that genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether the 3D marks are disclosed in U.S. Patent Nos. 6,993,858 and 7,146,751; whether Crocs has touted the functionality of the 3D marks in advertising; whether commercial alternatives to the 3D marks are available; and whether the 3D marks result from a simpler or cheaper method of manufacture.
n152.quote: Here, there are genuine issues of material fact with respect to the Morton-Norwich factors. Specifically, there are factual disputes as to whether (1) the 3D marks are disclosed in U.S. Patent Nos. 6,993,858 and 7,146,751; (2) Crocs has touted the functionality of the 3D marks in its

n153.point: The ALJ applied the legal standard for summary determination, requiring that there be no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party be entitled to determination as a matter of law, with evidence viewed in the light most favorable to the opposing party.
n153.quote: Summary determination is appropriate when there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and the moving party is entitled to a determination as a matter of law. See 19 C.F.R. § 210.18.

n161.point: Crocs, Inc. is the complainant, a Delaware corporation headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado, founded in 2002. n161.quote: Crocs is a Delaware corporation with its headquarters and principal place of business in Broomfield, Colorado.

n162.point: Crocs asserted three trademark registrations: U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,149,328 (the '328 Registration), U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,273,875 (the '875 Registration), and U.S. Trademark Registration No. 3,836,415 (the '415 Registration). n162.quote: Crocs asserts three trademarks: (1) U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,149,328 (\"the '328 Registration\"); (2) U.S. Trademark Registration No. 5,273,875 (\"the '875 Registration\"); and (3) U.S. Trademark Registration No. 3,836,415 (\"the '415 Registration\").

n163.quote: The products at issue in this investigation are \"casual footwear with holes in the upper and such footwear's packaging.\"

n164.point: The Commission investigated whether casual footwear and packaging thereof violated Section 337 by reason of infringement of U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 3,836,415; 5,149,328; and 5,273,875, and whether a domestic industry existed as required by Section 337(a)(2).
n164.quote: [W]hether there is a violation of subsection (a)(1)(C) of section 337 in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation , or the sale within the United States after importation of certain products . . . by reason of infringement of one or more [U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 3,836,415; 5,149,328; and 5,273,875]

n165.point: The '328 Registration claims a three-dimensional configuration of the upper of a shoe comprising a pattern of 13 round holes on the horizontal portion and a textured strip on the vertical portion with 7 trapezoidal openings. The '875 Registration includes these elements plus a textured strip on the heel and a decorative band along the heel strap.
n165.quote: The mark consists of a three dimensional configuration of the outside design of an upper for a shoe comprising a pattern of 13 round holes on the horizontal portion of the upper of the shoe and a textured strip along the vertical portion of the upper having a pattern of 7 trapezoidal openings.

n166.point: The ALJ found that U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 5,149,328 and 5,273,875 (the 3D marks) are invalid because they have not acquired secondary meaning, though they are not functional and not generic.
n166.quote: 14. U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 5,149,328 and 5,273,875 are invalid. 15. U.S. Trademark No. 3,836,415 is valid.

n167.point: The Trademark Office initially rejected Crocs' applications to register the overall look of the Classic Clog as generic, finding that the elements are commonly present in waterproof strap clogs and that applicant cannot exclude competitors from using such ubiquitous design elements. Crocs then narrowed its claimed design elements to specific ventilation holes.
n167.quote: These features are nondistinctive and do not function as a mark because such elements are so common in the industry for such products and are the same or substantially similar to the designs of competitors' products such that consumers are accustomed to seeing such elements on similar products.

n168.point: The ALJ found that U.S. Trademark Registrations 5,149,328 and 5,273,875 are not functional under the four-factor Morton-Norwich test, which examines utility patents, advertising, manufacturing, and availability of alternative designs.
n168.quote: 12. U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 5,149,328 and 5,273,875 are not functional.

n169.point: The ALJ found that the 3D marks and word mark are not generic, meaning they do not refer to a genus of goods or services rather than indicating a particular source.
n169.quote: 13. The Asserted Trademarks are not generic.

n17.point: Crocs alleges trademark infringement under Section 32(1) of the Lanham Act, false designation of source/unfair competition under Section 43(a), and dilution under Section 43(c) of the Lanham Act with respect to the Asserted Trademarks.
n17.quote: Respondents have also violated Section 337(a)(1)(A) by engaging in unfair methods of competition, false designations of source, and/or likely dilution of one or more trademarks that Crocs uses in connection with the Crocs Shoes.

n170.point: The ALJ concluded that the Orly Gator and Orly Redesign products do not infringe the Asserted Trademarks, based on analysis of the DuPont factors for likelihood of confusion.
n170.quote: 4. The Orly Accused Products do not infringe the Asserted Trademarks.

n171.point: The ALJ concluded that the Hobby Lobby Accused Products do not infringe the Asserted Trademarks.
n171.quote: 5. The Hobby Lobby Accused Products do not infringe the Asserted Trademarks.

n172.point: The ALJ concluded that the Orly, Hobby Lobby, and Amoji accused products do not falsely designate their source or cause unfair competition.
n172.quote: 8. The Orly Accused Products do not falsely designate their source or cause unfair competition.

n173.point: The ALJ concluded that respondents do not dilute the Asserted Trademarks, including findings on dilution by blurring and dilution by tarnishment.
n173.quote: 11. Respondents do not dilute the Asserted Trademarks.

n174.point: The ALJ found that the technical prong of the domestic industry requirement has been satisfied for the Asserted Trademarks, meaning Crocs' domestic activities satisfy the requirement that the products be covered by the asserted intellectual property rights.
n174.quote: 17. The technical prong of the domestic industry requirement has been satisfied for the Asserted Trademarks.

n175.point: From 2018 to 2021, Crocs' domestic investments in plant and equipment and labor and capital totaled a substantial amount. The ALJ found these investments quantitatively large in absolute terms and qualitatively significant, as the Classic Clog is critical to Crocs' business and its U.S.-based design and development employees are essential to the company's success.
n175.quote: From 2018-2021, Crocs' domestic industry investments in plant and equipment and labor and capital totaled [amount]. These domestic investments are quantitatively large in absolute terms, and on that basis satisfy the economic prong of the domestic industry requirement.

n176.point: The ALJ found that the economic prong of the domestic industry requirement is satisfied under 19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(3)(A) and (B) based on Crocs' significant plant and equipment investments and labor and capital expenditures related to its unlined Classic Clog product in the United States.
n176.quote: 18. The economic prong of the domestic industry requirement has been satisfied with respect to the Asserted Patents.

n177.point: The ALJ determined that no violation of Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has occurred based on infringement of the asserted trademarks and that there is no violation under 19 U.S.C. § 1337(a)(1)(A).
n177.quote: For the reasons stated herein, I have determined that no violation of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, has occurred in the importation into the United States, the sale for importation, or the sale within the United States after importation of certain casual footwear and packaging thereof alleged to infringe U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 3,836,415; 5,149,328; and 5,273,875.

n178.point: Because no violation of Section 337 was found, the ALJ recommends against a general exclusion order, limited exclusion orders, and cease and desist orders. However, the ALJ provided conditional recommendations regarding the form of relief should the Commission on review find a violation.
n178.quote: Because no violation of section 337 has occurred, I recommend against a GEO. Should the Commission disagree, however, the record demonstrates that a GEO is necessary to prevent circumvention of a limited exclusion order and there is a widespread pattern of infringement.

n179.point: Should the Commission determine that a violation has occurred, the ALJ recommends that limited exclusion orders issue against the Accused Products found to infringe, with a carve-out for respondents' footwear affirmatively found not to infringe the Asserted Trademarks.
n179.quote: Should the Commission determine that a violation has occurred, I recommend entry of a limited exclusion order against the Accused Products found to infringe.

n18.point: Crocs has established a domestic industry with both technical and economic prongs. The technical prong is satisfied by Crocs designing and developing Crocs Shoes in the United States that practice the Asserted Trademarks. Over the past three years, Crocs sold more than 23 million pairs generating $521.4 million in revenue in 2020, more than 12 million pairs generating $248.4 million in 2019, and more than 7.5 million pairs generating $131.8 million in 2018.
n18.quote: Over the past three calendar years, for example, Crocs has sold: more than 23 million pairs of Crocs Shoes and generated $521.4 million in revenue in 2020; more than 12 million pairs of Crocs Shoes and generated $248.4 million in revenue in 2019; and more than 7.5 million Crocs Shoes; and generated $131.8 million in revenue in 2018.

n180.point: The ALJ recommends cease and desist orders against Orly, Hobby Lobby, and Amoji if the Commission determines a violation has occurred, based on their commercially significant inventories or significant domestic operations that could undercut the remedy provided by an exclusion order.
n180.quote: Based on these facts, I recommend that a cease and desist order issue as to Orly if the Commission determines that a violation of section 337 has occurred.

n181.point: If an exclusion order issues, the ALJ recommends that bond be set at a specified amount per shoe during the 60-day Presidential review period to protect Crocs from injury, based on a price differential calculation between the Accused Products and the domestic industry products.
n181.quote: It is therefore my recommendation that the Commission set bond at [amount] per shoe during the Presidential review period.

n182.point: The ALJ found that Crocs' word mark CROCS (Registration No. 3,836,415) is valid and has reached incontestable status as of August 25, 2010, meaning the registration is conclusive evidence of the validity of the registered mark.
n182.quote: The Word Mark has reached incontestable status. JX-0003 at 152-158, 169, 182-188, 192 (declarations of incontestability and use); JX-0004 at CROCS_ITC045682; 15 U.S.C. § 1065; 15 U.S.C. § 1115(b)

n183.quote: 1. The Commission has subject matter, personal, and in rem jurisdiction in this investigation. 2. The importation or sale requirement of section 337 has been satisfied.

n184.quote: The Commission instituted this investigation on July 9, 2021, based on a complaint filed by Crocs, Inc. of Broomfield, Colorado

n185.quote: infringement, false designation of origin, and dilution of one of more of U.S. Trademark Registration Nos. 5,149,328; 5,273,875 (collectively, the "3D Marks"); and 3,836,415 ("the Word Mark")

n187.quote: named numerous respondents, including: Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. of Oklahoma City, Oklahoma

n188.quote: The ID also finds that Crocs has satisfied both the technical and economic prongs of the domestic industry ("DI") requirement

n189.quote: On January 9, 2023, the ALJ issued the subject ID finding no violation of section 337 because: (1) Crocs failed to prove that any of Respondents infringes the 3D Marks

n191.quote: The Commission has determined not to review the remaining findings in the ID.

n198.quote: Explain whether the evidence of record demonstrates that the shoes that were allegedly the subject of Orly's first sale practiced the 3D Marks in question

n200.quote: the Commission has determined that there has been no violation of section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930

n202.quote: The Commission has also determined to set a bond in the amount of one hundred (100) percent of the entered value of infringing goods imported during the period of Presidential review.

n203.quote: The Commission finds that the public interest factors do not preclude entry of such relief.

n204.quote: Commissioner Kearns joins Parts I, II, III, IV, and V.A. of this Opinion but otherwise respectfully dissents from the Commission's decision

n205.point: The asserted 3D marks consist of specific design elements of a shoe upper: the ʼ328 Mark claims a pattern of 13 round holes in the horizontal portion and 7 trapezoidal holes in the vertical portion; the ʼ875 Mark includes those same elements plus a textured strip on the heel and a decorative band along the heel strap.
n205.quote: The mark consists of a three dimensional configuration of the outside design of an upper for a shoe comprising a pattern of 13 round holes

n206.point: The accused products are the Orly Gator, Orly Redesign, and Amoji Garden Clogs (including Revised Garden Clogs), all casual footwear with holes in the upper; Orly also used the mark 'GATOR' and Hobby Lobby used the mark 'CROC,' both accused of infringing the word mark 'CROCS'.
n206.quote: Crocs accuses the 'Orly Gator' and 'Orly Redesign,' below, of infringing the 3D Marks.

n207.point: Crocs asserted the lined and unlined versions of its Classic Clog include the 3D Marks and take the Commission's position on whether Crocs satisfied the domestic industry requirement, neither confirming nor denying Crocs's satisfaction of the technical and economic prongs.
n207.quote: Crocs asserts the lined and unlined versions of its Classic Clog include the 3D Marks.

n208.point: The ALJ found that the 3D Marks do not cover the entirety of the shoe or its overall look because the overall look of a clog is a common or generic design element not entitled to trademark protection.
n208.quote: do not cover the entirety of the shoe or its overall look.' Id. at 5 (emphasis in ID).

n209.point: During prosecution of the ʼ328 Mark, the trademark examiner stated that the overall clog shape, defined midsole, and topline collar represent generic elements commonly present in waterproof strap clogs that are nondistinctive and do not function as marks, and only the specific shape and placement of ventilation/draining holes are potentially capable of distinguishing Crocs's goods.
n209.quote: The remaining elements of the proposed configuration which appear potentially capable of distinguishing applicant's goods comprise the specific shape and placement of ventilation/draining holes.

n21.point: Crocs' Classic Clog was conceptualized as a boat shoe and became recognized by 2005 as a standard-bearer in fashion footwear, professional footwear, and casual lifestyle footwear markets. The shoe's distinctive appearance features holes and textured elements that form the basis of the 3D Marks.
n21.quote: Crocs' iconic Classic Clog was conceptualized during a sailing trip and originally presented to consumers as a boat shoe. Soon after, it became apparent that the shoe appealed to consumers of all demographics seeking fun and friendly, comfortable footwear.

n210.point: The Commission affirmed the ALJ's finding that Crocs failed to prove that Orly, Hobby Lobby, or Amoji infringe the 3D Marks or Word Mark, finding that the Orly/Hobby Lobby Gator has a similar overall commercial appearance to the 3D Marks but the Orly/Hobby Lobby Redesign and Amoji Garden Clog do not.
n210.quote: the Commission affirms the ID's findings that Orly, Hobby Lobby, and Amoji do not infringe the 3D Marks or Word Mark

n211.point: With respect to DuPont factor 2 (similarity and nature of goods), the Commission adopted the ALJ's finding that this factor favors likelihood of confusion because the products are all EVA clogs or molded clog-type footwear, but declines to elevate this factor and assigns it lesser weight because the trademark examiner found the clog to be a common generic feature.
n211.quote: the Commission affirms the ID's finding that this factor favors finding a likelihood of confusion because the Orly Gator, Orly Redesign, Amoji Garden Clog, and Classic Clog are all EVA clogs

n212.point: With respect to DuPont factor 4 (conditions of sale), the Commission affirmed that this factor weighs against likelihood of confusion because accused shoes have different tags and price points than Crocs Classic Clogs, with Orly Gators retailing for $6-10 at Hobby Lobby versus $40 or more for Classic Clogs.
n212.quote: retail price of $6-10 for Orly Gators at Hobby Lobby vs. $40 or more for Classic Clogs

n213.point: With respect to DuPont factor 5 (fame of mark), the Commission modified the ALJ's finding to determine this factor is neutral rather than weighing against likelihood of confusion, but agreed that Crocs's evidence of fame for the 3D Marks is weak, as distinguished from general recognition of the common clog design.
n213.quote: the Commission modifies the ID to find this factor is neutral; it does not weigh against the likelihood of confusion.

n214.point: With respect to DuPont factors 7, 8, and 12 (actual confusion), the Commission found that Crocs's alleged evidence of actual confusion is ambiguous and weak, consisting only of two social media posts referring to purchasing 'crocs' at Hobby Lobby which may have used the term generically rather than as a trademark, and testimony from Orly's former Chief Operating Officer that was corrected upon closer review and provided little evidence of real-life consumer confusion.
n214.quote: These two posts refer to purchasing 'crocs' at Hobby Lobby, which suggests they were using the term generically, although this is not clear.

n215.point: The Commission found that Dr. Pittaoulis's consumer survey was unreliable because her control image (a black mesh slide) bore little resemblance to the non-trademarked elements of the test stimuli, such as the overall clog shape and heel strap, rendering it impossible to determine whether survey respondents were reacting to the absence of the 3D Marks or to the absence of many other unclaimed features.
n215.quote: the ID correctly finds that Dr. Pittaoulis's control shoe did not share many of the non-trademarked design elements of the test shoe, which rendered her survey unreliable and non-probative.

n216.point: The Commission rejected Crocs's argument that gross association rates (65-75%) alone can establish likelihood of confusion, finding that gross association rates lack a control to filter out unwanted influences and that over half of Dr. Pittaoulis's survey respondents erroneously associated even a black mesh slide with Crocs despite its substantial differences from the 3D Marks or Classic Clog.
n216.quote: The Commission disagrees. Gross association rates alone, which by definition lack a control to filter out unwanted influences, make it very difficult, if not impossible, to determine

n217.point: With respect to DuPont factor 9 (variety of goods), the Commission modified the ALJ's finding to determine this factor is neutral rather than weighing against likelihood of confusion, noting that where a trademark is not used on a variety of goods or services, the TTAB has held this factor should be viewed as neutral.
n217.quote: the Commission finds this factor is neutral. Not even Crocs, however, argues that this factor should weigh in favor of likelihood of confusion.

n218.point: The Commission affirmed the ALJ's finding that Crocs failed to prove that respondents falsely designated the source or origin of the accused products, which is an unfair act under Section 337(a)(1)(A).
n218.quote: Crocs Failed to Show False Designation of Origin

n219.point: The Commission took no position on the ALJ's findings regarding secondary meaning and the presumption of validity for the 3D Marks, as well as findings that respondents failed to prove the 3D Marks are functional or that the Word Mark is generic.
n219.quote: The Commission takes no position on Orly's alleged first sale, the presumption of validity, secondary meaning, fair use, injury, and the technical and economic prongs of domestic industry.

n22.point: The Crocs 3D Marks are non-functional. They feature one-of-a-kind ornamental design characteristics giving the impression of a fun and distinctively quirky clog-like shoe. The distinctively gentle slope of the upper gives the shoe a unique, recognizable outline, and competitors have virtually infinite non-infringing footwear styles available.
n22.quote: They 3D Marks feature one-of-a-kind ornamental design characteristics that give the overall impression of a fun and distinctively quirky clog-like shoe for which Crocs is well-known. The distinctively gentle slope of the upper gives the shoe a unique, recognizable outline.

n220.point: The ALJ found that respondents failed to prove the 3D Marks are invalid as functional, and the Commission took no position on this finding or on respondents' fair use defense.
n220.quote: The ID also finds that Respondents failed to prove that the 3D Marks are invalid as functional or the Word Mark is invalid as generic.

n221.point: The Commission reversed the ALJ's finding that Crocs waived its infringement contentions with respect to the lined versions of the Orly Gator, finding that Crocs's pre-hearing brief expressly referenced both lined and unlined versions of the Orly Gators and alleged they were substantially similar to the 3D Marks.
n221.quote: The Commission has determined to reverse the ID's finding of waiver with respect to the lined Orly Gators

n222.point: The Commission reversed the ALJ's finding that Crocs waived its infringement contentions against the four defaulting respondents (La Modish, Star Bay, Huizhou, and Anao), finding that this waiver doctrine does not apply to issuance of an LEO or CDO against a party found in default pursuant to 19 U.S.C. § 1337(g)(1).
n222.quote: the Commission has determined to set aside the ID's findings with respect to waiver as they do not apply to issuance of an LEO or CDO against a party found in default

about.text: The complainant is Crocs, Inc., a Delaware company based in Broomfield, Colorado, that makes and sells the Classic Clog and other footwear worldwide. The Commission's notice of investigation, issued in July 2021 on Crocs' complaint, named a large number of respondents -- footwear brands, importers, and retailers such as Cape Robbin, Orly Shoe Corp., Hobby Lobby Stores, Walmart, PW Shoes, Quanzhou ZhengDe Network Corp. (d/b/a Amoji), Fujian Wanjiaxin Industrial Developing (a/k/a Wanjiaxin), Maxhouse Rise, Loeffler Randall, and others based in the United States, China, Hong Kong, and Brazil. The case concerns alleged copying of the look of Crocs' clog-style shoes -- footwear with round holes across the top of the foot and a textured strip with trapezoidal openings along the side, some also with a textured heel strip and decorative heel-strap band -- as well as use of the CROCS name.

Crocs asserted three federal trademark registrations: the '328 and '875 registrations, which are three-dimensional ('3D') marks protecting the specific design of holes, textured strip, and (for the '875 mark) heel details on the shoe upper, and the '415 registration, a word mark for 'CROCS.' The 3D marks were registered in 2017 based on use since 2003; the word mark was registered in 2010 based on use since 2002. The Commission instituted the investigation to determine whether the importation and sale of the accused footwear and its packaging violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act, the statute that lets the Commission block imports that infringe intellectual property rights, by infringing these marks or through false designation of source or trademark dilution.

allegations.text: Crocs alleges that the accused products -- clog-style shoes sold by respondents such as Cape Robbin, Orly, Hobby Lobby, Amoji, and others, manufactured abroad (including in China and Brazil) and imported into the United States for sale through retailers and online platforms -- copy the design features protected by the 3D marks, including the size, positioning, number and shape of the holes and the textured heel and strap elements. Crocs alleges this importation and sale constitutes trademark infringement, false designation of source, and dilution in violation of Section 337, pointing to customer reviews referring to accused shoes as 'crocs' as evidence of actual confusion.

To bring a Section 337 case a complainant must show a domestic industry -- U.S. activity tied to the asserted right. Crocs alleges it satisfies this requirement because it designs and develops its Classic Clog and other Crocs Shoes bearing the asserted marks in the United States, selling over 23 million pairs for $521.4 million in 2020 alone, and because it makes significant investments in plant, equipment, labor, capital, and research and development directed to products practicing the marks.

Crocs seeks a general exclusion order -- an order barring the entry of infringing goods regardless of source, as opposed to a limited exclusion order aimed only at named respondents -- arguing that a pattern of violation and difficulty identifying the source of many infringing imports justifies broad relief, or in the alternative a limited exclusion order together with cease-and-desist orders, which would bar named U.S. respondents from selling their existing U.S. inventory of infringing goods.

paragraphs.text: PW Shoes denies infringing any valid trademark and denies that the asserted marks are valid, arguing they are generic, functional, and lack secondary meaning (the association consumers must make between a design and a single source for it to work as a trademark). PW also denies domestic industry, denies any likelihood of confusion, and raises waiver, estoppel, and laches, contending Crocs is not entitled to a general exclusion order or cease-and-desist orders.

Orly Shoe Corporation (with Hobby Lobby also named in this answer) denies that its White Foam Clog or other products infringe, and denies that the 3D marks are valid, asserting they are functional, merely ornamental, generic, and lacking distinctiveness or secondary meaning, with the underlying registrations subject to cancellation. Orly also disputes domestic industry, arguing Crocs cannot show the required investment in plant, equipment, labor, or capital tied to the marks, and raises laches, abandonment, unclean hands, antitrust misuse, and fair use.

paragraphs.text: Walmart denies violating Section 337 and denies that the accused products infringe the 3D marks, arguing they are not substantially similar to generic foam clogs sold by Walmart and that there is no likelihood of confusion given differences in price, channels of trade, and lack of fame. Walmart also contends the 3D marks are invalid as functional, ornamental, generic, and lacking secondary meaning, that Crocs cannot establish domestic industry on either the technical or economic prong, and raises fair use, laches, unclean hands, and public-interest objections, seeking a finding of no violation and attorneys' fees.

Fujian Wanjiaxin (with Maxhouse Rise also named) denies infringing any valid trademark, arguing the accused products are generic foam clogs not substantially similar to the 3D marks and that there is no likelihood of confusion given differences in appearance, price, and lack of fame. Wanjiaxin contends the marks are functional (citing Crocs' own touting of ventilation benefits), ornamental, generic, and without secondary meaning, disputes domestic industry on both prongs, and raises fair use, laches, and unclean hands, seeking denial of all relief.

decisions.text: In the final initial determination, the ALJ found that the 3D marks ('328 and '875) are invalid for lack of secondary meaning, though not functional and not generic; the word mark ('415) was found valid and incontestable. The ALJ found that the remaining accused products -- the Orly Gator and Orly Redesign shoes, the Hobby Lobby products, and the Amoji Garden Clogs and Redesigns -- did not infringe the 3D marks or the word mark, did not falsely designate source, and did not dilute the marks by blurring or tarnishment. The ALJ found that Crocs had satisfied both the technical and economic prongs of the domestic industry requirement, based on Crocs' substantial U.S. investment in designing and developing the Classic Clog. Because no infringement was found, the ALJ concluded there was no violation of Section 337, while making conditional recommendations that, if the Commission found a violation, limited exclusion orders and cease-and-desist orders should issue against Orly, Hobby Lobby, and Amoji, with a bond set by a price-differential calculation.

On review, the Commission determined not to review most of the ALJ's findings, including domestic industry and the functionality/genericness rulings, but reviewed and affirmed the ALJ's ultimate finding that Crocs failed to prove infringement, false designation of origin, or dilution by Orly, Hobby Lobby, or Amoji. The Commission agreed the Orly/Hobby Lobby Gator shoe had overall similar commercial appearance to the 3D marks but that the Redesign and Amoji Garden Clog did not, and found Crocs' evidence of actual confusion (two social-media posts and corrected witness testimony) weak, and its consumer survey unreliable because its control image did not properly isolate the trademarked design elements. The Commission modified some individual likelihood-of-confusion factors (finding fame and variety-of-goods neutral rather than against confusion) but the overall no-infringement result stood. The Commission also reversed the ALJ's finding that Crocs had waived certain infringement contentions, both as to lined Orly Gator shoes and as to the four defaulting respondents, but this did not change the ultimate outcome for the participating respondents. Commissioner Kearns dissented in part, stating he would have found the 3D marks acquired secondary meaning and would have remanded on domestic industry.

Because four respondents -- La Modish Boutique, Star Bay Group, Huizhou Xinshunzu, and Jinjiang Anao Footwear -- had been found in default and did not participate in the litigated findings, the Commission issued a limited exclusion order and cease-and-desist orders against them despite finding no violation as to the litigating respondents, reasoning that the waiver doctrine applied to Crocs' proof did not bar relief against defaulting parties. The Commission set the bond during the period of Presidential review at 100 percent of the entered value of infringing goods, and found the public interest factors did not preclude this relief.

summary.headline: In Investigation No. 337-TA-1270, Crocs, Inc. accused numerous makers, importers, and sellers of "casual footwear with holes in the upper" (and its packaging) of infringing Crocs' registered trademarks covering the design of its Classic Clog and the CROCS word mark; after most respondents settled or defaulted, the Commission found no violation by the three respondents who litigated to decision (Orly, Hobby Lobby, and Amoji) but issued a limited exclusion order and cease-and-desist orders against four defaulting respondents.

rulings.text: Before the hearing, respondent Loeffler Randall moved for summary determination -- a ruling without trial where there is no genuine factual dispute -- that its footwear was not substantially similar to the asserted marks and therefore did not infringe. Crocs and the investigative staff opposed. The ALJ found genuine issues of material fact remained on substantial similarity and denied the motion, leaving non-infringement for trial.

Walmart, Orly, Hobby Lobby, and ZhengDe later moved for a ruling that Crocs' 3D trade dress was functional and therefore invalid as a matter of law, pointing to two Crocs utility patents covering the shoe design as strong evidence of functionality. Applying the Morton-Norwich test (which looks at utility patents, advertising claims, alternative designs, and manufacturing cost) and the general standard for summary determination, the ALJ found disputed facts on whether the marks were disclosed in the patents, whether Crocs had touted functional benefits, and whether alternative designs and cheaper manufacturing methods existed, and denied the motion.

ZhengDe separately moved for partial summary determination of non-infringement as to certain alternative footwear designs it had developed. Applying a four-factor ripeness test from a prior Commission case (whether a product is within the investigation's scope, has been imported, is fixed in design, and has been disclosed in discovery), the ALJ found Crocs disputed three of the four factors and that genuine issues of fact remained, denying the motion.

standing.text: The investigation is terminated. Most originally named respondents left the case through settlement or consent orders -- among them Cape Robbin, SG Footwear, Dr. Leonard's, Fullbeauty, Legend Footwear, Fujian Huayuan Well, Bijora, Hawkins Footwear, Shoe-Nami, PW Shoes, 718Closeouts, Dongguan Eastar, KGS Sourcing, Maxhouse Rise and Wanjiaxin, Mould Industria de Matrizes, Royal Deluxe Accessories, Loeffler Randall, Skechers, and Walmart. Four respondents -- La Modish Boutique, Star Bay Group, Huizhou Xinshunzu Shoes, and Jinjiang Anao Footwear -- were found in default and are subject to a limited exclusion order and cease-and-desist orders (against La Modish and Star Bay) with a 100-percent bond. As to the three respondents who litigated to a decision -- Orly Shoe Corp., Hobby Lobby Stores, and Quanzhou ZhengDe Network Corp. (Amoji) -- the Commission found no violation of Section 337: Crocs did not prove infringement, false designation of origin, or dilution of the 3D marks or the CROCS word mark, so no exclusion order or cease-and-desist order issued against them. The Commission took no position on several underlying findings, including secondary meaning, the presumption of validity for the 3D marks, and whether Crocs satisfied the economic prong of domestic industry, and Commissioner Kearns dissented in part from the Commission's opinion.
